# Adrelisse Pellavreth, PhD, MPH

Professor of Cardiovascular Epidemiology and Director, Rural Cardiovascular Research Unit  
Veylorn Ridge Academic Health Center, West Virginia, United States  
Curriculum vitae updated 30 September 2026

## Education and appointments

Dr. Pellavreth received a BS in statistics from Keldavren College in 1996, an MPH in epidemiology from Ordelvane Institute of Public Health in 1998, and a PhD in epidemiology from the same institution in 2003. Her dissertation examined differences between routinely recorded and standardized blood-pressure measurements in adult outpatient care. She completed a postdoctoral appointment in health services research at Veylorn Ridge Academic Health Center from 2003 to 2005.

Her appointments at Veylorn Ridge have been Assistant Professor, 2005–2011; Associate Professor, 2011–2018; and Professor, 2018–present. She has directed the Rural Cardiovascular Research Unit since 2019. Veylorn Ridge is an academic health center with outpatient services, graduate research training, and an institutional review board. It is organizationally separate from the community clinic network described in this dossier.

## Research experience

Dr. Pellavreth studies hypertension care in rural adult populations, with particular attention to measurement conditions, medication access, follow-up, and the interpretation of routine clinical records. Her work combines clinic-based quantitative studies with interviews conducted by community health workers and qualitative researchers. She has served as principal investigator on pragmatic intervention research and as an epidemiologic collaborator on observational analyses of adult primary care.

She was principal investigator of the Veylorn Rural Medication and Pressure Study, abbreviated V-RMAPS. This completed study examined pharmacist-led management in rural primary-care clinics. She was responsible for the protocol, allocation procedures, analysis oversight, research governance, and final reporting. A licensed pharmacist directed medication management; Dr. Pellavreth did not prescribe or make individual treatment decisions. Her main analytic responsibilities included defining the blood-pressure endpoint, assessing differential follow-up, and interpreting the limitations of a small number of randomized clinics.

Her qualitative experience includes developing interview guides with community health workers, reviewing coding frameworks, and integrating interview findings with clinic-level implementation records. She is not the team's lead qualitative interviewer. That responsibility belongs to Dr. Tessavelle Brindelvane, whose training and work are described in the team record.

## Completed research support

**V-RMAPS: Veylorn Rural Medication and Pressure Study.** Veylorn Community Care Research Trust, award VCCRT-20-047; principal investigator, Adrelisse Pellavreth; 1 January 2021–31 December 2024. The completed award totaled $576,000, comprising $480,000 in direct costs and $96,000 in indirect costs. The final scientific report was accepted on 28 February 2025, and the financial account is closed. This was foundation support, not an NIH award. No unspent award balance remains available to the unit.

Current unit salaries, record retention, and equipment maintenance receive institutional support. This support is not recorded as an external research grant, and the unit does not describe the completed V-RMAPS award as current funding. From award closeout through September 2026, her work on V-RMAPS has concerned dissemination, approved secondary analysis, and archive oversight; recruitment and intervention delivery have not resumed.

## Teaching, supervision, and scope of expertise

Dr. Pellavreth teaches graduate epidemiologic methods and supervises work on missing outcome data and measurement in routine care. She chairs the health center's research measurement working group. Her publications through September 2026 are listed separately, with distinctions between published work and a manuscript still under review.

Her direct recruitment and intervention experience concerns adults receiving primary care. Neither she nor the current research team has recruited adolescents, conducted research in schools, or completed a sleep research study. Her completed V-RMAPS cohort contained no participant younger than 30 years. She has not supervised actigraphy processing, polysomnography, circadian phase assessment, or adolescent assent procedures. These activities are not included among her established research competencies.

# Final scientific report: Veylorn Rural Medication and Pressure Study

**V-RMAPS; reporting period 1 January 2021–31 December 2024**  
Principal investigator: Adrelisse Pellavreth, PhD, MPH  
Host: Veylorn Ridge Academic Health Center  
Funder: Veylorn Community Care Research Trust, VCCRT-20-047  
Final report accepted: 28 February 2025  
Archive copy and closeout status reviewed: 30 September 2026

## Purpose and setting

V-RMAPS evaluated pharmacist-led blood-pressure management embedded in rural adult primary care. The study addressed medication reconciliation, treatment adjustment under collaborative practice agreements, and practical barriers to follow-up. Celdavreth Trace Community Clinics contributed eight clinics: four in West Virginia and four in Kentucky. These clinics served rural catchment areas and used the same electronic health record platform, although staffing patterns and appointment capacity differed.

The project was a pragmatic cluster-randomized clinical trial. Clinics were allocated in a 1:1 ratio, with four assigned to pharmacist-led management and four to usual care. Allocation was stratified by state, giving two clinics per study arm in each state. An independent statistician generated the allocation sequence after clinic participation agreements were signed. The protocol and primary analysis specification were deposited in the health center's dated research archive before allocation.

## Participants and procedures

Recruitment ran from 1 July 2021 to 30 June 2022. The study enrolled 480 patients, with 60 at each clinic and 240 in each arm. Participants were aged 30–79 years, had a recorded hypertension diagnosis, and had uncontrolled blood pressure confirmed at a research measurement visit. The age eligibility criteria excluded adolescents and adults younger than 30. Recruitment used clinic lists, clinician referrals, telephone invitations, and community health worker follow-up. Schools were not recruitment sites or referral partners.

The intervention offered pharmacist medication review and management during a six-month follow-up period. Pharmacists could recommend or implement medication changes within their signed collaborative practice agreements. Community health workers assisted with appointment reminders, transport arrangements, and communication about medication access. Usual-care clinics continued their existing clinical services. Both groups received the same research measurement schedule; neither participants nor clinical staff were blinded to allocation.

The primary endpoint was standardized seated systolic blood pressure at six months, adjusted for baseline systolic blood pressure and the state allocation stratum. Trained research assistants obtained three upper-arm readings after five minutes of seated rest and averaged the last two. Cuff size was selected from measured arm circumference. Staff documented recent smoking, caffeine consumption, and deviations from the measurement procedure. Whenever staffing allowed, the endpoint assessor was someone other than the participant's community health worker, but assessor masking was not assured.

The final six-month assessment window closed on 31 January 2023. Record reconciliation, qualitative analysis, and workflow assessment continued during the remaining award period. The quantitative database was locked on 30 September 2024.

## Participant accounting and blood-pressure results

Standardized six-month measurements were obtained for 408 of 480 (85.0%) participants. Follow-up was completed by 208 of 240 (86.7%) in the pharmacist arm and 200 of 240 (83.3%) in usual care. The Wilson 95% confidence interval for overall retention was 81.5%–87.9%. The 72 participants without a standardized endpoint comprised 68 participants alive at six months with missing measurements and four who died before six months. Among the 68 survivors with missing measurements, 36 could not be contacted, 20 declined the endpoint visit, and 12 moved outside the service area. Deaths were recorded as all-cause terminal events, distinct from missing measurements among survivors; the trial was not designed to estimate mortality effects.

Baseline systolic blood pressure averaged 153.2 mmHg, with a standard deviation of 12.4 mmHg, across all 480 participants. Arm-specific baseline means were 153.6 mmHg in pharmacist clinics and 152.8 mmHg in usual-care clinics. Among participants with paired research measurements, the unadjusted mean change was −11.4 mmHg in the pharmacist arm and −5.1 mmHg in usual care. These descriptive changes use the retained participants and are not the primary between-arm effect estimate.

The adjusted between-arm difference in six-month systolic blood pressure was −6.0 mmHg (95% CI −9.8 to −2.2), favoring pharmacist-led management. The prespecified linear mixed model included a clinic random intercept and used a small-sample degrees-of-freedom correction. Participants were analyzed according to their clinic's allocation. The primary estimate used the 408 observed standardized endpoints and represents an adjusted contrast among participants who survived and attended the endpoint assessment, rather than a treatment effect for all 480 enrollees.

The four deaths were handled as terminal events and were not assigned or imputed six-month blood-pressure values. The multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis was restricted to the 476 participants alive at six months, imputing the 68 missing measurements among those survivors. It estimated a survivor-conditional adjusted contrast of −5.5 mmHg (95% CI −9.6 to −1.4). Imputation included clinic, allocation, baseline blood pressure, age, and available routine follow-up measurements. This analysis assumed missingness was explainable by the observed variables among survivors. It did not establish robustness to unmeasured reasons for nonattendance. Both this contrast and the observed-endpoint analysis may be affected by post-randomization survival and attendance selection and do not estimate a treatment effect for all 480 enrollees. Neither estimate establishes a reduction in cardiovascular events.

## Records, interviews, and workflow findings

Electronic record linkage succeeded for 456 of 480 (95.0%) participants. Of the 24 unresolved linkages, 16 involved inactive legacy records and eight involved identifier discrepancies that could not be resolved within the approved linkage procedure. Successful linkage meant a verified match to a clinical record; it did not mean that every follow-up field was complete or that a standardized endpoint had been obtained. Routine blood-pressure readings were not substituted for missing primary endpoints.

The qualitative component included 32 individual interviews: 20 patients, six clinic staff members, and six community health workers. Sampling sought variation in attendance and clinic location rather than statistical representativeness. Participants described transport dependence, uncertainty about medication costs, difficulty reaching the clinic by telephone, and discomfort discussing missed doses. Staff described repeated reconciliation work when medication lists differed between clinical encounters. These were interpreted themes, not prevalence estimates. Interviews were recorded with consent, transcribed, and coded using a shared framework with documented disagreement resolution.

A separate workflow exercise involved 18 clinic staff members using a paper prototype for reconciling community blood-pressure records. In the first session, 12 of 18 (66.7%) completed the matching task without assistance. After revisions to labels and field order, 16 of 18 (88.9%) completed it without assistance in a second session. The same staff attended both sessions. These descriptive results are susceptible to practice effects and do not demonstrate improved patient blood pressure. No treatment allocation or medication changes were part of this workflow exercise.

## Limitations and closeout

The trial included only eight clinics within one network. Shared leadership and a common record system limit transferability to independently governed practices. Patient and staff masking was infeasible, and differences in contact intensity may have influenced follow-up. The retention difference and the small number of clusters constrain interpretation despite the prespecified analysis and sensitivity assessment.

The study measured office blood pressure and care processes. It did not collect objective sleep measurements, sleep diaries, sleep timing, sleep duration, or sleep regularity. It also did not collect research-grade physical activity monitoring, ambulatory blood pressure, or a biospecimen collection. The project provides no adolescent data and no evidence about recruiting through schools.

As of 30 September 2026, intervention delivery and recruitment remain ended. The award account is closed, while approved retention and secondary analysis of study records continue. No additional participants or follow-up measurements have been added since the database lock. The published main analysis, interview paper, linkage paper, and the separately identified workflow manuscript are documented in the publications list.

# Publications and manuscript status

Rural Cardiovascular Research Unit, Veylorn Ridge Academic Health Center  
Record checked: 30 September 2026

The following four articles are published. Author order, titles, publication years, and DOI strings below are the unit's bibliographic record. All concern adult rural primary care or methods used in that setting. None reports adolescent recruitment, school-based research, or sleep measurement.

## Published articles

**Pellavreth, A.; Norravick, C.; Ellsvareth, N.; Arvendrel, L.; Brindelvane, T. (2022).** Pharmacist-led blood-pressure management in rural primary care: protocol for the V-RMAPS cluster-randomized trial. *Veylorn Journal of Rural Cardiovascular Practice*, 7(2), 81–93. DOI: 10.99999/pb.rural-hypertension-group.2022.1

This protocol describes clinic allocation, adult eligibility, pharmacist responsibilities, the standardized blood-pressure endpoint, and the original analysis specification. It contains no outcome results. The participant age range begins at 30 years. Its description of community health worker involvement concerns appointment support and contact through adult clinics, not recruitment through educational institutions.

**Brindelvane, T.; Densavren, R.; Ellsvareth, N.; Pellavreth, A. (2024).** Medication access and follow-up in rural hypertension care: interviews with patients, clinic staff, and community health workers. *Ordelvane Community Care Methods*, 11(3), 144–158. DOI: 10.99999/pb.rural-hypertension-group.2024.1

This article reports the interview component of V-RMAPS. It includes the sampling rationale, coding process, and accounts of transport, cost uncertainty, telephone access, and medication reconciliation. The findings describe experiences among purposively selected interview participants. The article does not estimate the proportion of all clinic patients who encounter each barrier.

**Pellavreth, A.; Arvendrel, L.; Norravick, C.; Ellsvareth, N.; Brindelvane, T.; Densavren, R. (2025).** Six-month blood-pressure outcomes of pharmacist-led management in eight rural clinics: the V-RMAPS trial. *Veylorn Journal of Rural Cardiovascular Practice*, 10(1), 15–30. DOI: 10.99999/pb.rural-hypertension-group.2025.1

This is the primary outcome article. It reports the adjusted between-arm systolic blood-pressure difference, participant retention, and missing-data sensitivity analysis. The primary adjusted contrast was −6.0 mmHg (95% CI −9.8 to −2.2) among the 408 participants with observed endpoints, distinct from within-arm descriptive changes. The four deaths were treated as terminal events without assigned or imputed six-month blood-pressure values. Multiple imputation covered the 68 missing measurements among the 476 participants alive at six months, yielding a survivor-conditional adjusted contrast of −5.5 mmHg (95% CI −9.6 to −1.4) under an observed-variable missingness assumption among survivors. Both analyses may be affected by post-randomization survival and attendance selection and do not estimate a treatment effect for all 480 enrollees. Follow-up ends at six months; it does not establish durability after intervention completion or effects on cardiovascular events.

**Ellsvareth, N.; Arvendrel, L.; Pellavreth, A.; Densavren, R. (2026).** Reconciling research and electronic clinical records in a rural hypertension cohort. *Keldavren Health Services Measurement and Linkage*, 4(2), 62–76. DOI: 10.99999/pb.rural-hypertension-group.2026.1

This methods article describes verified record matches, unresolved identifiers, and differences between routine clinical readings and standardized research measurements. Its linkage success denominator is the enrolled cohort, not only participants retained at the endpoint visit. Successful linkage is not treated as evidence of complete longitudinal data. The paper documents the approved matching procedure without releasing direct patient identifiers.

## Manuscript under review

**Brindelvane, T.; Ellsvareth, N.; Densavren, R.; Pellavreth, A.** Staff use of a paper reconciliation form for community blood-pressure records: a repeated-session workflow assessment. Submitted to *Ordelvane Community Care Methods* on 18 August 2026; under review as of 30 September 2026.

This manuscript has not been accepted or published and has no assigned DOI. It reports the repeated-session exercise with clinic staff described in the final report. The unit's publication count above excludes this submission. No journal endorsement or peer-reviewed validation of these workflow findings is claimed.

# Team and community relationships

Rural Cardiovascular Research Unit, Veylorn Ridge Academic Health Center  
Current record: 30 September 2026

## Core staff

**Adrelisse Pellavreth, PhD, MPH — unit director and cardiovascular epidemiologist.** Dr. Pellavreth leads study governance and quantitative interpretation. She has experience coordinating pragmatic adult clinic research and integrating standardized measurements with health services data. Her current appointment is salaried by the health center. She is not a physician, and the unit does not assign her clinical prescribing responsibilities.

**Calverin Norravick, PharmD — clinical pharmacy lead.** Norravick supervised medication review and pharmacist documentation during V-RMAPS. His work included checking reconciliation records, documenting treatment recommendations, and maintaining communication with primary-care clinicians. He retains a clinical appointment at Veylorn Ridge. His completed research experience is in adult hypertension care. He has no pediatric research appointment and has not delivered a sleep intervention or interpreted clinical sleep studies.

**Tessavelle Brindelvane, PhD — qualitative health services researcher.** Brindelvane led the interview analysis and workflow exercise. Her methods include semistructured interviews, framework analysis, observation of clinical workflows, and cognitive testing of paper forms. She maintained the coding decision log and separated participant accounts from staff interpretations. She has worked with adults in clinical and community meeting settings; her research record does not include interviewing minors or conducting school-based fieldwork.

**Lurencio Arvendrel, MS — biostatistician.** Arvendrel maintains the analysis archive and contributed to the mixed-model and missing-data analyses. His experience includes clustered clinical data, small-sample inference, and reproducible record linkage checks. He has not developed or validated algorithms for actigraphy, sleep staging, circadian phase estimation, or wearable-derived sleep regularity.

**Naomelle Ellsvareth, MPH — research operations and data manager.** Ellsvareth coordinated clinic agreements, staff measurement training, endpoint tracking, and reconciliation of research and electronic records. She maintains the data dictionary and access log. Her experience concerns consent by adults with capacity to consent. The unit has no completed experience administering adolescent assent and parental permission procedures.

**Ruthavelle Densavren — community health worker coordinator.** Densavren supervises the community health worker network and maintains contact with clinic coordinators. She helped develop interview language and procedures for contacting participants who missed visits. Her role includes participant navigation and community communication, not medication prescribing or independent clinical diagnosis.

These six people are current members of the unit. Their appointments do not constitute unrestricted availability: clinical duties, institutional teaching, and existing service responsibilities remain part of their work. There is no sleep scientist, pediatric investigator, or school liaison among the core staff, and no external collaborator in those specialties has a signed research agreement with the unit.

## Community health worker network

The current network comprises 12 community health workers: seven based in West Virginia and five in Kentucky. Densavren is one of the 12, not an additional worker. Members are employed by the clinic network or its community services arm rather than all being employees of Veylorn Ridge. Their present service responsibilities include helping adult patients navigate appointments, understand clinic instructions, and communicate practical barriers to care.

Workers received study-specific training in adult consent, standardized blood-pressure procedures, confidentiality, and escalation of concerning readings during V-RMAPS. Prior training does not confer permission to collect data for another study. The network has no experience recruiting adolescents, recruiting within schools, or administering sleep research devices. Existing contacts are adult patients, clinic personnel, and community service organizations; they are not a school recruitment infrastructure.

## Clinic partnership and community input

Celdavreth Trace Community Clinics remains a service partner across the same eight clinics. Its standing memorandum with Veylorn Ridge supports staff liaison, discussion of completed findings, and institutionally approved record retention. It remains in force as of 30 September 2026. It does not provide standing permission to enroll patients or release identifiable records for new research.

A community advisory group includes former adult participants, caregivers, and clinic representatives. It reviewed the wording of V-RMAPS participant materials and helped interpret practical barriers reported in interviews. It is advisory rather than a consent authority or a source of guaranteed enrollment. Neither the clinic memorandum nor the advisory group's membership includes a school district, youth organization, or adolescent-serving research partner.

# Existing facilities, equipment, and data holdings

Veylorn Ridge Academic Health Center, Rural Cardiovascular Research Unit  
Inventory and access statement: 30 September 2026

## Measurement equipment and space

The unit owns 24 automated upper-arm blood-pressure monitors of a model independently validated for adult clinical measurement. Sixteen are assigned to clinic measurement rooms, with two at each participating clinic, and eight are stored centrally for training and replacement. The inventory includes adult cuffs covering arm circumferences from 22 to 52 cm. Equipment logs record cuff condition, device checks, and removal from use when readings or physical inspection indicate a problem. Adult validation and cuff availability are not documented as pediatric validation.

All 24 monitors remain in the inventory after V-RMAPS closeout. They are spot-measurement instruments, not ambulatory blood-pressure monitors. Their readings do not measure sleep, physical activity, or circadian phase. Research assistants have a written seated blood-pressure procedure and competency checklist used during the completed study. Community readings require documentation of location, posture, cuff size, and recent activity because these conditions are not uniformly controlled outside clinic rooms.

The health center provides secure interview rooms, an encrypted audio recorder, transcription software, and a restricted-access analysis environment. Clinic rooms belong to Celdavreth Trace and remain subject to clinical scheduling. Their use during the completed trial does not reserve them for other research activities.

The unit owns no actigraphs, polysomnography equipment, sleep-specific wearable devices, or ambulatory blood-pressure monitors. No such equipment is on order. There is no sleep laboratory within the unit, and no signed access agreement with an external sleep laboratory. The equipment inventory contains no instruments represented as already available for objective sleep assessment.

## V-RMAPS data archive

The retained archive contains 480 baseline participant records, 408 standardized six-month blood-pressure endpoints, and verified electronic record links for 456 participants. These counts refer to overlapping groups rather than additive samples. A participant can have a verified clinical record link while lacking the standardized endpoint. The archive retains flags distinguishing research measurements from routine readings and documents the reasons for unresolved matches.

Available baseline fields include age, sex recorded in the clinical record, hypertension treatment, standardized blood pressure, and reported difficulty attending appointments. Routine records contain encounter dates, medication lists, and clinical blood-pressure entries with variable completeness. The archive also includes the interview coding framework, redacted interview transcripts, workflow observation sheets, the analysis specification, and executable analysis scripts. Interview transcripts are not treated as anonymous merely because names have been removed; accounts of local services can still be identifying.

No participant in the archived cohort was younger than 30 at enrollment. The archive contains no adolescent observations, no participants aged 18–29, and no school-level information. It has no objective sleep records, sleep diaries, sleep timing variables, sleep-duration variables, or sleep-regularity measures. Encounter timestamps describe healthcare contacts and have not been validated as proxies for sleep or circadian behavior. There are no retained research biospecimens or standardized research lipid or glycemic measurements.

## Access, permissions, and present status

The clinical record custodian is Celdavreth Trace Community Clinics. Veylorn Ridge maintains the research copy under the completed study's data-use agreement and institutional review board approval. As of 30 September 2026, that agreement and approval remain applicable to record retention and approved secondary analyses; they do not authorize resumed enrollment or intervention delivery. The linkage key is held separately from the analysis files. Approved unit analysts have access through named accounts; the community health worker network has no general access to research analysis files.

The original consent covered the completed trial, its specified interviews, record linkage, and approved secondary analyses of hypertension care. It did not authorize unrestricted recontact, school recruitment, or collection of additional physiological measurements. New participant contact and new data collection require their own institutional determination and applicable permissions. The archived dataset is controlled access and is not an openly downloadable resource.

The original study is closed to enrollment and intervention delivery. Retained records remain subject to the approved retention schedule, access controls, and disclosure review. Existing institutional computing support covers storage and maintenance of the completed archive. The closed foundation award provides no continuing funds, and clinic partnership status does not transfer ownership of clinical records to the research unit.

R-MAPS evaluated pharmacist-led blood-pressure management embedded in rural adult primary care. The study addressed medication reconciliation, treatment adjustment under collaborative practice agreements, and practical barriers to follow-up. Cedar Trace Community Clinics contributed eight clinics: four in West Virginia and four in Kentucky. These clinics served rural catchment areas and used the same electronic health record platform, although staffing patterns and appointment capacity differed.

The project was a pragmatic cluster-randomized clinical trial. Clinics were allocated in a 1:1 ratio, with four assigned to pharmacist-led management and four to usual care. Allocation was stratified by state, giving two clinics per study arm in each state. An independent statistician generated the allocation sequence after clinic participation agreements were signed. The protocol and primary analysis specification were deposited in the health center's dated research archive before allocation.

## Participants and procedures

Recruitment ran from 1 July 2021 to 30 June 2022. The study enrolled 480 patients, with 60 at each clinic and 240 in each arm. Participants were aged 30–79 years, had a recorded hypertension diagnosis, and had uncontrolled blood pressure confirmed at a research measurement visit. The age eligibility criteria excluded adolescents and adults younger than 30. Recruitment used clinic lists, clinician referrals, telephone invitations, and community health worker follow-up. Schools were not recruitment sites or referral partners.

The intervention offered pharmacist medication review and management during a six-month follow-up period. Pharmacists could recommend or implement medication changes within their signed collaborative practice agreements. Community health workers assisted with appointment reminders, transport arrangements, and communication about medication access. Usual-care clinics continued their existing clinical services. Both groups received the same research measurement schedule; neither participants nor clinical staff were blinded to allocation.

The primary endpoint was standardized seated systolic blood pressure at six months, adjusted for baseline systolic blood pressure and the state allocation stratum. Trained research assistants obtained three upper-arm readings after five minutes of seated rest and averaged the last two. Cuff size was selected from measured arm circumference. Staff documented recent smoking, caffeine consumption, and deviations from the measurement procedure. Whenever staffing allowed, the endpoint assessor was someone other than the participant's community health worker, but assessor masking was not assured.

The final six-month assessment window closed on 31 January 2023. Record reconciliation, qualitative analysis, and workflow assessment continued during the remaining award period. The quantitative database was locked on 30 September 2024.

Standardized six-month measurements were obtained for 408 of 480 (85.0%) participants. Follow-up was completed by 208 of 240 (86.7%) in the pharmacist arm and 200 of 240 (83.3%) in usual care. Deaths were recorded as all-cause events; the trial was not designed to estimate mortality effects.

These descriptive changes use the retained participants and are not the primary between-arm effect estimate.

The adjusted between-arm difference in six-month systolic blood pressure was −6.0 mmHg (95% CI −9.8 to −2.2), favoring pharmacist-led management. The prespecified linear mixed model included a clinic random intercept and used a small-sample degrees-of-freedom correction. Participants were analyzed according to their clinic's allocation. The primary estimate used the 408 observed standardized endpoints and therefore depends on assumptions about outcome availability.

A sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation for missing endpoints gave an adjusted difference of −5.5 mmHg (95% CI −9.6 to −1.4). Imputation included clinic, allocation, baseline blood pressure, age, and available routine follow-up measurements. This analysis assumed missingness was explainable by the observed variables. It did not establish robustness to unmeasured reasons for nonattendance. Neither estimate establishes a reduction in cardiovascular events.

## Records, interviews, and workflow findings

Electronic record linkage succeeded for 456 of 480 (95.0%) participants. Of the 24 unresolved linkages, 16 involved inactive legacy records and eight involved identifier discrepancies that could not be resolved within the approved linkage procedure. Successful linkage meant a verified match to a clinical record; it did not mean that every follow-up field was complete or that a standardized endpoint had been obtained. Routine blood-pressure readings were not substituted for missing primary endpoints.

The qualitative component included 32 individual interviews: 20 patients, six clinic staff members, and six community health workers. Sampling sought variation in attendance and clinic location rather than statistical representativeness. Participants described transport dependence, uncertainty about medication costs, difficulty reaching the clinic by telephone, and discomfort discussing missed doses. Staff described repeated reconciliation work when medication lists differed between clinical encounters. These were interpreted themes, not prevalence estimates. Interviews were recorded with consent, transcribed, and coded using a shared framework with documented disagreement resolution.

A separate workflow exercise involved 18 clinic staff members using a paper prototype for reconciling community blood-pressure records. In the first session, 12 of 18 (66.7%) completed the matching task without assistance. After revisions to labels and field order, 16 of 18 (88.9%) completed it without assistance in a second session. The same staff attended both sessions. These descriptive results are susceptible to practice effects and do not demonstrate improved patient blood pressure. No treatment allocation or medication changes were part of this workflow exercise.

## Limitations and closeout

The trial included only eight clinics within one network. Shared leadership and a common record system limit transferability to independently governed practices. Patient and staff masking was infeasible, and differences in contact intensity may have influenced follow-up. The retention difference and the small number of clusters constrain interpretation despite the prespecified analysis and sensitivity assessment.

The study measured office blood pressure and care processes. It did not collect objective sleep measurements, sleep diaries, sleep timing, sleep duration, or sleep regularity. The project provides no adolescent data and no evidence about recruiting through schools.

The trial included only eight clinics within one network. Shared leadership and a common record system limit transferability to independently governed practices. Patient and staff masking was infeasible, and differences in contact intensity may have influenced follow-up. The retention difference and the small number of clusters constrain interpretation despite the prespecified analysis and sensitivity assessment.

The study measured office blood pressure and care processes. It did not collect objective sleep measurements, sleep diaries, sleep timing, sleep duration, or sleep regularity. It also did not collect research-grade physical activity monitoring, ambulatory blood pressure, or a biospecimen collection. The project provides no adolescent data and no evidence about recruiting through schools.

As of 30 September 2026, intervention delivery and recruitment remain ended. The award account is closed, while approved retention and secondary analysis of study records continue. No additional participants or follow-up measurements have been added since the database lock. The published main analysis, interview paper, linkage paper, and the separately identified workflow manuscript are documented in the publications list.

Veylorn Ridge Academic Health Center, Rural Cardiovascular Research Unit  
Inventory and access statement: 30 September 2026

## Measurement equipment and space

The unit owns 24 automated upper-arm blood-pressure monitors of a model independently validated for adult clinical measurement. Sixteen are assigned to clinic measurement rooms, with two at each participating clinic, and eight are stored centrally for training and replacement. The inventory includes adult cuffs covering arm circumferences from 22 to 52 cm. Equipment logs record cuff condition, device checks, and removal from use when readings or physical inspection indicate a problem. Adult validation and cuff availability are not documented as pediatric validation.

All 24 monitors remain in the inventory after V-RMAPS closeout. They are spot-measurement instruments, not ambulatory blood-pressure monitors. Their readings do not measure sleep, physical activity, or circadian phase. Research assistants have a written seated blood-pressure procedure and competency checklist used during the completed study. Community readings require documentation of location, posture, cuff size, and recent activity because these conditions are not uniformly controlled outside clinic rooms.

The health center provides secure interview rooms, an encrypted audio recorder, transcription software, and a restricted-access analysis environment. Clinic rooms belong to Celdavreth Trace and remain subject to clinical scheduling. Their use during the completed trial does not reserve them for other research activities.

The unit owns no actigraphs, polysomnography equipment, sleep-specific wearable devices, or ambulatory blood-pressure monitors. No such equipment is on order. There is no sleep laboratory within the unit, and no signed access agreement with an external sleep laboratory. The equipment inventory contains no instruments represented as already available for objective sleep assessment.

## V-RMAPS data archive

The retained archive contains 480 baseline participant records, 408 standardized six-month blood-pressure endpoints, and verified electronic record links for 456 participants. These counts refer to overlapping groups rather than additive samples. A participant can have a verified clinical record link while lacking the standardized endpoint. The archive retains flags distinguishing research measurements from routine readings and documents the reasons for unresolved matches.

Available baseline fields include age, sex recorded in the clinical record, hypertension treatment, standardized blood pressure, and reported difficulty attending appointments. Routine records contain encounter dates, medication lists, and clinical blood-pressure entries with variable completeness. The archive also includes the interview coding framework, redacted interview transcripts, workflow observation sheets, the analysis specification, and executable analysis scripts. Interview transcripts are not treated as anonymous merely because names have been removed; accounts of local services can still be identifying.

No participant in the archived cohort was younger than 30 at enrollment. The archive contains no adolescent observations, no participants aged 18–29, and no school-level information. It has no objective sleep records, sleep diaries, sleep timing variables, sleep-duration variables, or sleep-regularity measures. Encounter timestamps describe healthcare contacts and have not been validated as proxies for sleep or circadian behavior. There are no retained research biospecimens or standardized research lipid or glycemic measurements.

## Access, permissions, and present status

The clinical record custodian is Celdavreth Trace Community Clinics. Veylorn Ridge maintains the research copy under the completed study's data-use agreement and institutional review board approval. The original consent covered the completed trial, its specified interviews, record linkage, and approved secondary analyses of hypertension care. It did not authorize unrestricted recontact, school recruitment, or collection of additional physiological measurements. The archived dataset is controlled access and is not an openly downloadable resource.

The original study is closed to enrollment and intervention delivery. Retained records remain subject to the approved retention schedule, access controls, and disclosure review. The closed foundation award provides no continuing funds, and clinic partnership status does not transfer ownership of clinical records to the research unit.

facts.text: Adrelisse Pellavreth leads the Rural Cardiovascular Research Unit at Veylorn Ridge Academic Health Center in West Virginia, United States.
Pellavreth has held a professor appointment since 2018 and has directed the unit since 2019.
Pellavreth completed her BS in 1996, MPH in 1998, PhD in 2003, and postdoctoral appointment during 2003–2005.

Foundation award VCCRT-20-047 supported V-RMAPS from 1 January 2021 through 31 December 2024 with $576,000 total funding, comprising $480,000 direct and $96,000 indirect costs, and is financially closed with no remaining balance.
V-RMAPS was a completed cluster-randomized clinical trial involving eight clinics, four in each state and four in each study arm, with two clinics per arm within each state.
V-RMAPS recruited 480 adults aged 30–79 during July 2021–June 2022, with 60 participants per clinic and 240 per arm, and completed its final six-month assessment window on 31 January 2023.
Six-month retention was 408 of 480 participants, or 85.0% with a Wilson 95% confidence interval of 81.5%–87.9%, including 208 of 240 in pharmacist care and 200 of 240 in usual care.
The 72 missing standardized endpoints comprised 36 participants who could not be contacted, 20 who declined assessment, 12 who moved away, and four who died.

Baseline systolic blood pressure averaged 153.2 mmHg with standard deviation 12.4 mmHg overall, with arm means of 153.6 and 152.8 mmHg, while paired unadjusted changes were −11.4 mmHg in pharmacist care and −5.1 mmHg in usual care.

The primary adjusted between-arm difference in six-month systolic blood pressure was −6.0 mmHg with a 95% confidence interval from −9.8 to −2.2, estimated using 408 observed endpoints and a clinic random-intercept model with a small-sample correction.

The multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis estimated an adjusted difference of −5.5 mmHg with a 95% confidence interval from −9.6 to −1.4 under an assumption that missingness was explainable by observed variables.
Record linkage succeeded for 456 of 480 participants, or 95.0%, while 16 inactive legacy records and eight unresolved identifier discrepancies accounted for the 24 unsuccessful matches.

The qualitative component comprised 32 interviews with 20 patients, six clinic staff, and six community health workers and identified transport, cost uncertainty, telephone access, and medication reconciliation barriers without estimating their population prevalence.

In a repeated-session workflow exercise with 18 staff, unaided task completion increased from 12 of 18, or 66.7%, to 16 of 18, or 88.9%, after form revisions, with practice effects unresolved and no patient blood-pressure effect measured.

The unit lists four published articles from 2022, 2024, 2025, and 2026, while its workflow manuscript submitted on 18 August 2026 remained under review on 30 September 2026 with no acceptance or assigned DOI.
The six current core members cover cardiovascular epidemiology, clinical pharmacy, qualitative health services research, biostatistics, research operations, and community health worker coordination.
The community health worker network has 12 members, including coordinator Ruthavelle Densavren, with seven based in West Virginia and five in Kentucky.

Celdavreth Trace Community Clinics remains a partner across eight clinics under a memorandum in force as of 30 September 2026 that does not authorize new patient enrollment or release of identifiable records.
The unit owns 24 adult-validated upper-arm blood-pressure monitors, with 16 assigned as two per clinic and eight held centrally, and adult cuffs covering arm circumferences of 22 to 52 cm.

The controlled-access archive holds 480 baseline records, 408 standardized endpoints, 456 verified record links, redacted interview transcripts, workflow records, and analysis scripts, with the participant groups overlapping rather than additive.
Neither Pellavreth nor the current team has recruited adolescents or conducted school research, and their completed V-RMAPS cohort contained no participant younger than 30.

The core team has no sleep scientist, pediatric investigator, school liaison, or signed external research collaborator in those specialties, and has no completed adolescent assent and parental permission experience.

The unit has no actigraphs, polysomnography equipment, sleep-specific wearables, ambulatory blood-pressure monitors, equipment orders for those instruments, or signed external sleep-laboratory access agreement.

The archive contains no adolescent or age-18–29 observations, objective sleep records, sleep diaries, timing, duration or regularity measures, school-level information, retained biospecimens, or standardized research lipid or glycemic measurements.

review_issues.problem: The report puts deaths among the 72 absent endpoints and then describes imputation for missing endpoints under an ordinary observed-variable missingness assumption, without saying how deaths were treated or what population the BP contrast targets. Six-month BP after death does not exist; it cannot simply be treated as an unobserved living-person measurement. The supplied sensitivity estimate is therefore scientifically ambiguous, especially because the stretch brief explicitly asks the writer to build on this missing-data expertise.
review_issues.fix: Make the fictional historical analysis explicit: 'The four deaths were handled as terminal events and were not assigned or imputed six-month BP values. The multiple-imputation analysis was restricted to the 476 participants alive at six months, imputing the 68 missing measurements among those survivors. It estimated a survivor-conditional adjusted contrast of −5.5 mmHg (95% CI −9.6 to −1.4), under an observed-variable missingness assumption among survivors. Both this contrast and the observed-endpoint analysis may be affected by post-randomization survival/attendance selection and do not estimate a treatment effect for all 480 enrollees.' Distinguish terminal events from missing measurements in F08 and carry the restricted population and limitations into F10/F11 and the primary-publication summary.
